segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when we could bear it no longer, we thought it best to be left behind in Athens alone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s coworker in the good news of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you for the sake of your faith,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no one would be shaken by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that this is what we are appointed for.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Indeed, when we were with you, we kept telling you in advance that we were going to suffer affliction—and so it happened, as you know.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith, for fear that the tempter had somehow tempted you and our labor would turn out to be for nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now Timothy has come to us from you and has brought us the good news of your faith and love. He has told us that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, just as we long to see you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and affliction we were encouraged about you through your faith,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for now we live, if you are standing firm in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what thanks can we give back to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before our God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as night and day we pray with the utmost earnestness to see you face to face and to supply what is lacking in your faith?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And may the Lord make you increase and overflow in love for one another and for everyone, just as we do for you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so as to strengthen your hearts to be blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his holy ones.

notes.phrase: we thought it best to be left behind in Athens alone
notes.note: The letter is sent by Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, and it is unclear whether “we” here means Paul and Silvanus together or is Paul’s way of speaking of himself. Verse 5 repeats the same statement in the singular (“I sent”), which leads many interpreters to think Paul mainly means himself. The translation keeps the Greek’s plural and singular as they stand.

Manuscripts differ here: some read “God’s servant” (or “minister”), some “God’s coworker,” and some combine the two. Most scholars think “God’s coworker” is original and that scribes softened so bold a description. The phrase could also be taken as “our coworker for God,” but the plainer sense is that Timothy works alongside God.

The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which today is heard as a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

This verb occurs only here in the New Testament. Its earlier use was of a dog wagging its tail, and from that of fawning or flattering, so some interpreters take the sense to be “beguiled” or “talked out of their faith” by smooth words. Most translators and lexicons take the meaning here to be “disturbed” or “unsettled,” which is followed in the text.

The word is often rendered “tribulation,” which many readers now hear as the name of a specific end-time period. In the period it was an ordinary word for hardship or oppression pressing on someone, here the hostility the Thessalonians met from their neighbors. “Affliction” is itself a long-established rendering, and the related verb in verse 4 is translated “suffer affliction” to keep the link visible.

Paul uses the same verb he normally reserves for announcing the message about Christ. This is the only place in his letters where it refers to other good news, and the choice of word shows how much Timothy’s report meant to him.

The Greek plural, traditionally “brothers” or “brethren,” was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as members of one family. Since Paul is addressing the whole congregation, “brothers and sisters” conveys what the first hearers understood. Several modern translations do the same; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

The prayer has two subjects, “our God and Father” and “our Lord Jesus,” but the Greek verb is singular. Greek can use a singular verb with a compound subject, so the grammar alone proves little, but many interpreters note how closely Paul joins God and Jesus as the one to whom prayer is addressed. The word “himself” could grammatically cover both subjects or the Father alone.

The Greek word means arrival and the presence that follows. It was commonly used for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city, an occasion that involved public preparation and welcome. Paul uses it in this letter for the expected arrival of Jesus as Lord.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul normally uses the word for all believers, but here many scholars think it refers to angels accompanying the Lord, echoing Zechariah 14:5 (“the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him”). Others take it as believers who have died, or as both together; “holy ones” leaves the question open, as the Greek does. Some manuscripts add “Amen” at the end of the verse.

candidates.reason: The plural address to congregations recurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translations split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so one policy is needed.
The verb ranges over encourage, comfort, urge and appeal across the New Testament, and readers lose the link with παράκλησις and παράκλητος if the English varies without a rule.
Recurs in Luke, Acts, Paul, the Catholic letters and Revelation, with translations varying between “strengthen,” “establish” and “confirm.”
Paul’s regular term for his associates, variously rendered “fellow worker,” “coworker,” “helper” and “partner” in English versions.
It is paired with θλῖψις and στενοχωρία in several lists of hardships and also means “necessity” or “compulsion” elsewhere, so the sense split and the English for each need fixing.
